content: Trimethoprim is a widely used antibacterial agent with a half-life ranging from 8 to 11 hours. The toxic dose or serum level of trimethoprim is not well established. However, toxic levels of this drug can lead to bone marrow suppression, methemoglobinemia, and hyperkalemia. The mechanism of action of trimethoprim involves the inhibition of folic acid synthesis in bacteria. It achieves this by blocking the activity of the bacterial enzyme dihydrofolate reductase. Humans, in contrast, do not synthesize their own folic acid, which explains the selective toxicity of trimethoprim against bacterial cells while sparing human cells. Trimethoprim exhibits bacteriostatic activity against a broad range of bacterial pathogens. Sulphonamides, the earliest class of antibacterial agents, also interfere with folic acid synthesis but act on a different enzyme in the pathway, dihydropteroate synthase, which precedes dihydrofolate reductase in the folic acid production process. Trimethoprim was originally developed and marketed as a potentiator for sulphonamides. Co-trimoxazole is a combination of trimethoprim and the sulphonamide sulfamethoxazole. This combination inhibits tetrahydrofolic acid synthesis at two consecutive steps in the pathway, resulting in an enhanced antibacterial effect in vitro compared to the effects of the individual components. However, this synergistic effect is more challenging to demonstrate in vivo. Pathogens that are resistant to both sulphonamides and trimethoprim are relatively rare, and the combination may exhibit bactericidal effects in some cases. Due to increasing bacterial resistance to sulphonamides and the heightened risk of adverse effects when used in combination—particularly the risk of severe reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome—trimethoprim is most commonly used as a single agent in the United Kingdom. The use of co-trimoxazole for the treatment of bacterial infections is no longer recommended in the UK.
